Newly emerged hatchlings of the Eastern mud turtle (Kinosternon subrubrum) possess a modest plastron length at birth of 1.84 centimeters [Lb = 1.84 centimeters], a dimension that reflects the species' relatively small egg size compared to other kinosternids. Incubation experiments conducted under controlled conditions at a constant 30.5 °C [T = 30.5 °C] reveal that the mean age at birth is 106 days [ab = 106 days], a developmental period consistent with the prolonged embryogenesis observed in many freshwater turtles inhabiting temperate climates. This thermal regime, typical of late-summer nest temperatures in the southeastern United States, appears to optimize the balance between developmental rate and hatchling quality. After emerging, these neonates quickly begin exogenous feeding on small aquatic invertebrates, initiating a growth trajectory that will span several years before reproductive maturity is attained. The relatively abbreviated incubation period at this temperature may confer a selective advantage by allowing hatchlings sufficient time to forage and build energy reserves before the onset of winter dormancy, a critical life-history stage for this species which occupies ephemeral wetlands subject to seasonal desiccation.

Females of Kinosternon subrubrum ultimately attain a maximum plastron length of 10.2 centimeters [Li = 10.2 centimeters], a value derived from extensive field surveys of adult specimens across the species' range. Males, in contrast, reach a smaller adult carapace size, with the ultimate plastron length for males asymptotically approaching 9 centimeters [Li = 9 centimeters], a pronounced sexual size dimorphism that is characteristic of the genus. This divergence in body size likely arises from differential selective pressures: larger body size in females enhances fecundity through greater abdominal volume for egg production, while males may benefit from smaller, more maneuverable bodies during aquatic courtship and inter-male agonistic encounters. In terms of absolute mass, the ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 209 grams [Wwi = approximately 209 grams] in fully grown individuals, a value comparable to that recorded for the closely related scorpion mud turtle but adjusted for the slightly smaller linear dimensions of K. subrubrum. This mass is achieved only after many years of steady somatic growth in productive wetland habitats.

The attainment of reproductive capability in this species is closely tied to a threshold body dimension. Field studies indicate that puberty, or the onset of gonadal maturation, occurs when females have reached a plastron length of 7.75 centimeters [Lp = 7.75 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds to a several-year post-hatching interval. Under ambient thermal conditions averaging 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the time since birth at puberty for this species has been estimated at approximately 6.3 years since birth [tp = approximately 6.3 years since birth], representing a substantial delay before females begin investing in egg production. This protracted pre-reproductive period is common among long-lived freshwater turtles and is thought to reflect the energetic demands of reaching a body size sufficient to support efficient reproductive output. Delayed maturity also reduces intra-specific competition between adults and juveniles, potentially stabilizing population dynamics in resource-limited environments. The age at which this plastron length is achieved can vary by a year or more depending on local productivity and the duration of the active foraging season.

Reproductive output in Eastern mud turtles is partitioned across multiple nesting events each active season. Females typically lay between one and six eggs per clutch, with a mean clutch size of approximately 3 eggs [N_R_i = clutch size of approximately 3 eggs], and they may produce up to three clutches per year [F_R_i = up to three clutches per year] when conditions are favorable. Under a thermal regime of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], this translates into a maximum annual reproductive rate of roughly six to eighteen eggs deposited per female over the course of the breeding season. Clutch size is positively correlated with maternal body size, such that larger females, having reached the ultimate plastron length, contribute disproportionately to annual recruitment. These eggs are typically deposited in shallow nests excavated in sandy or loamy soils adjacent to the aquatic habitat, where they incubate for a period influenced by local temperatures. The relatively high fecundity associated with multiple clutches may buffer against high rates of nest predation or environmental stochasticity.

Longevity data for Kinosternon subrubrum, compiled from both mark-recapture studies and captive maintenance records, indicate that the maximum lifespan for this species under natural conditions is approximately 40 years [am = approximately 40 years] when maintained at an average environmental temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This considerable lifespan, which exceeds that of many similarly sized freshwater turtles, is characteristic of a slow-paced life history strategy that balances delayed maturity and modest annual reproductive effort against high adult survival. The species' ability to persist for several decades is likely facilitated by its defensive morphology, including a hinged plastron that allows near-complete shell closure, and by its exploitation of relatively predator-safe aquatic refugia. Older individuals often exhibit signs of shell wear and epibiont accumulation, providing visible evidence of their advanced age. Such longevity underscores the importance of protecting adult survivorship in management plans, as population growth rates in this species are highly sensitive to adult mortality.
